stops.name: Karidoel, the Court of Bertane
stops.campa: Where the lake water pools beneath the walls at Nantua, in the mountain country above the Ain, stands Karidoel, the castle Werner Greub gives to Wolfram's King Arthur of Bertane, a land carved from the broken empire of Charlemagne's grandsons. Here Arthur holds his court and his Round Table, and here Queen Guinevere keeps her ladies about her. Bertane is a young kingdom, stitched together from the ruin of Louis the Pious's sons' wars, and Karidoel is its beating heart: a hall of falconers and minstrels, of oaths sworn and fellowship kept, waiting for the stranger knights this restless age is about to send it.

stops.name: Karidoel, the Blood Before the Gate
stops.campa: Before the gate a stranger knight, Ither of Kukumerlant, all in red, has spilled a golden cup over Guinevere's lap and ridden off unpunished, no man of Arthur's circle daring the field. A boy fresh from the forest of Soltane, ignorant of arms and their names, begs leave of the queen and rides after him bearing only a herdsman's javelin. He casts it through eye and neck; Ither falls dead on the grass before Nantes. Weeping over the body whose armor he cannot unbuckle, the boy is armed in the dead man's red mail by the squire Iwanet, and rides on: Ither's slayer and his heir both.
stops.quote: There the javelin swiftly sped, and thro' eye and neck it struck him, and the knight on the plain lay dead... So the armour was reft from the dead man, 'fore Nantes on the grassy plain, and they did it upon the living, o'er whose dealings did folly reign.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book III, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)

stops.name: Karminal, the Hunting Lodge
stops.campa: North of Bertane, above the young river Birs, rises Karminal, the hunting lodge Greub sets in the deep wood Wolfram calls Brizljan: the castle later ages will call Dorneck. Arthur keeps late summer here, hawks flown from the walls, hounds coursing the oak slopes toward the plain of the Birs below. It is a place between the court's pomp and the wild wood's law, half hall and half forest camp, and it is from here that Arthur's fellowship rides down toward the river, into whatever adventure the season sends among the falcons and the geese.

stops.name: The Oath Before the Search
stops.campa: For eight days Arthur's fellowship has ridden its own and stranger ground, hunting no game but a rumor: a Red Knight, unnamed, who has avenged them all on their old enemy Klamide without asking leave. Before the search goes further, Arthur calls in every man who can bear a shield and binds them by oath: whatever deeds of knighthood they may see, none shall venture a conflict without the king's own leave first given. Untrained hounds off the leash, he tells them, come to grief in strange country. It is the discipline of a court that means to make the unknown rider its own, and it will be sorely tested.
stops.quote: Now, 'tis well! Since we needs must go thro' many a stranger country, where many a stranger spear, and many a gallant hero are waiting us, I fear, if ye, like hounds untrainèd whose leash shall have slipped the hand of him who was late their master, shall roam free o'er all the land, much evil might there befall ye.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VI, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894), Arthur binding his knights before the search

stops.name: Down to the Birs
stops.campa: The fellowship breaks camp at Karminal and descends through the Brizljan wood toward the river, tents and wagons and the queen's household following the falconers down the old paths. By evening the army pitches along the Birs on the stretch the poem calls Plimizoel, below Dornachbrugg where the valley opens. A thousand tents and more go up, on either side of the water as the poem counts them; and because the Table itself can never be carried out of Nantes, the court brings instead the great round silk that stands for it, folded on a wagon like a relic going to its next altar.

stops.name: The Camp on the Plimizoel Meadow
stops.campa: The army lies strung along the Birs below the bridge at Dornachbrugg, and into this camp ride, one after another, the players of the coming drama: Orilus and his wronged sister Jeschute, Klamide the conquered king, Cunneware of Lalant and her champion. Arthur receives each with the courtesy that is his whole art of rule, seats the great among the small, and remembers old griefs kindly. Guinevere sits at his side through it all, queen of a camp that is, for these few autumn days, the true seat of Bertane. The falconers ride out hawking by the water at dusk, and one of the hawks does not come back.

stops.name: The Blood Drops in the Snow
stops.campa: Snow falls out of season on the woods above the camp, and Wolfram breaks in to say so: whatever men sing of Arthur happens at Whitsuntide or when May blossoms the meadow, never in snow. The lost falcon strikes a goose over a fallen tree; the bird escapes, and three drops of its blood fall crimson on the white ground. The young knight in red armor riding by, Parzival, reins in and cannot look away. White and red together are the face of his wife Kondwiramur, left at Pelrapeire. He sits his horse in a waking trance, lance upright, while the whole army watches and takes him for a challenger.
stops.quote: Say what hand hath painted these colours that here I see? Kondwiramur, I think well, these tints sure shall liken thee!... Red as blood-drops and white as the snowdrift, it rejoiceth me evermore!
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VI, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)

stops.name: Segramors Unhorsed
stops.campa: Cunneware's squire, riding out toward Lalant, spies the trance-bound stranger and turns back to cry shame on the camp for letting one knight sit unchallenged so near. Segramors, Guinevere's kinsman, tears the sable coverlet off the sleeping king and queen at dawn to beg leave, and the queen herself wins Arthur's grudging consent. He gallops out, taunts the silent knight, and charges; Parzival, whose wheeling horse swings the blood-drops out of his sight just long enough, wakes to answer the blow and unseats him in a single pass. Segramors picks himself from the snow more embarrassed than hurt, and the stranger sinks back at once into his waking dream.
stops.quote: Now it seemeth but ill to me that thus near our army lieth, and our presence rejoiceth thee!... I call on thee here to yield thee, ere I put thee to shame, Sir Knight!
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VI, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894), Segramors to the silent knight

stops.name: Keye's Fall
stops.campa: Kay the seneschal, stung by Segramors's shame, wins the same reluctant leave and rides out mocking, offers the entranced knight a hempen halter as to a runaway thief, and smites his helmet with the spear-shaft to wake him. Kay's lance does pierce the shield; the payment is swifter. Parzival's counter-blow throws horse and rider onto the same fallen tree where the geese had hidden, and Kay's right arm and left leg break between stone and saddle-bow, his girths and saddle and bells of gold shattered over the snow. Wolfram will not let him be despised for it: one blow, he says, repaid two, and the other was Cunneware's.
stops.quote: Sir Knight, since thou thus our king hast shamed, thou shalt hear my counsel, for wisdom perchance 'twill bring; thou shalt hang thee a hempen halter around thy neck straightway... Low on the snow I'll lay thee!
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VI, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894), Kay to the silent knight

stops.name: The Round Table Spread on the Plimizoel
stops.campa: Gawain ends the enchantment by the plainest means: he lays a cloth of silk and sendal over the blood-stained snow, and the spell goes out with the colors. Then Arthur has the second silk unrolled, the one woven in Acraton and carried from heathen lands, wide and shapen round, and spread on the flowering meadow where neither tree nor tent hinders it. The Table cannot be borne out of Nantes, so here they show its semblance. No high seat and no low; knight, lady and maiden alike are welcome at the ring. Arthur leads Parzival to it by the hand, and the fellowship is complete for one afternoon.
stops.quote: Then a silk in Acraton woven, they laid on the grassy sward, 'twas brought from far lands of paynim, and 'twas shapen both wide and round... No high seat had they of honour, but all men were equal there.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VI, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)

stops.name: Cundrie's Curse and the Call to Chastel Marveil
stops.campa: The honor lasts an afternoon. Cundrie the sorceress rides in on her mule, boar-tusked and bear-eared, speaking French to the Breton king, and before Arthur's whole circle denounces Parzival by name: he sat before the wounded Grail King Anfortas and asked no question of pity, and for that silence he is cursed. She shames Arthur too, telling him the fame of the Table suffered for the friendship it swore. Then she turns from them both to call any knight bold enough to ride to Chastel Marveil, where four queens and four hundred maidens lie captive, and rides on weeping.
stops.quote: Thou son of high Pendragon, thyself, and thy Breton host, by thy deed hast thou shamed... The fame of thy Table Round it suffered for the friendship ye with Parzival did swear... 'The Red Knight' ye here do call him, the name of one who lay dead before Nantes, yet I tell thee unlike in their life are they!
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VI, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)

stops.name: Kingrimursel's Challenge, and the Camp Broken
stops.campa: Before the shamed camp can recover, Kingrimursel, Landgrave of Schampfanzun, rides in and calls Gawain out by name to answer a charge of treason forty days hence in his own city; Gawain accepts and arms for departure. Then Ekuba, the young heathen queen of Janfuse, speaks up in the circle. Cundrie has already named the brother, she says; she can vouch for him, for she is his mother's cousin. He is Feirefis Angevin, king of Zassamank and Assagog, and his face is black and white together. By nightfall the camp breaks in three directions: Gawain toward his trial, Parzival toward the Grail, Arthur home to Karidoel.
